newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria lev stability seen hinged on quick reform.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria lev stability seen hinged on quick reform.

text.p: The Bulgarian lev's stability depends on how soon Bulgaria will be able to push ahead with radical reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and sustain an investor-friendly climate, bankers said.
The weekend election victory for the reformist Union of Democratic Forces boosted optimism about Bulgaria's economic prospects but hard work is still ahead of the new government.
The lev firmed to near 1,500 per dollar at early afternoon on Wednesday, up from 1,520-1,525 at Tuesday's close, as investors opting for high-yield government securities sold dollars, dealers said.

"There are good reasons why it can remain at this level and why it could weaken. Everything will depend on the actions taken by the government to make the economy more efficient," said Douglas Dryden, manager of the Raiffeisenbank Bulgaria branch.
"If they continue with the agressive implementation of the IMF plan, there is no reason to expect devaluation of the lev," he told Reuters.

The new government, due to take office in mid-May, faces the serious challenge of introducing a self-regulating restrictive monetary mechanism known as a currency board, intended to curb inflation and government spending, and stabilise the lev.

Under a $657 million reform and funding deal sealed by the IMF and an interim cabinet, Bulgaria pledged to introduce the currency board in June, speed up privatisation, and free prices and trade rules.

Interim Prime Minister Stefan Sofianski said recently the lev will be pegged to the anchor currency at a rate slightly lower than the current one. The IMF envisages an average lev/dollar rate for this year of 2,000.

Under the currency board system, the amount of levs in circulation must be matched precisely by the amount of foreign exchange reserves. Parliament has yet to vote on whether to peg the lev to the dollar or the mark.

First signs of stabilisation were seen after the two-month rule of the caretaker cabinet, which brought down monthly inflation to 12 percent in March from 243 percent in February and stopped the free fall of the lev from an all-time low of 3,000 per dollar in February.
Foreign investors, attracted by high yields and pending sell-offs, have stepped up the buying of Bulgarian government securities, with maturity over six months.
"Investors expect yield on Bulgarian paper to remain high, even if the lev is pegged at 2,000 to the dollar when the currency board system is introduced," an ING bank dealer said.
Bulgaria's central bank has encouraged local banks to sell the paper to boost their liquidity.
Yields to maturity on six- and 12-month floater coupon T-bills auctioned on Monday were 52.39 percent and 108.06 percent, respectively.
The coupons equalled the central bank main interest rate for the periods to maturity. The main interest rate is now set at 8.03 percent monthly.
Interest in dollar-denominated bad debt bonds, called Zunks, was persistently high because they could be used as a means of payment in sell-offs of state companies, a Post Bank dealer said.
"Once the currency board is in place and functioning, Bulgarian domestic debt instruments will remain an attractive investment and a less risky one than now," said a London-based dealer.
